toc.title: Would you want an objective measurement?
What your answer might tell you

blocks.p: If there was a magic pill you could take to activate your polyvagal state of safety and social engagement, would you? I asked that question of my email list and my community, and I want to explore it here with you too. Where are you with it, and what might be driving your answer? And then, what might next steps look like?

blocks.h: Would you want an objective measurement?

blocks.p: It started with vagal efficiency. The basic idea is that vagal efficiency measures how strong, how efficient, your vagal brake is: your safety state. So I asked my community: would you like to have an objective measurement?
I thought it'd be kind of cool. I'm the one creating the courses, so I like the idea of having an objective measure of whether these things are working. I got some really cool responses:

ul: One member said she'd be the first one to have her vagal efficiency measured. Maybe it's just curiosity, but she'd love to have some metrics to work with.

Another member said she has trouble registering what she's feeling, so an external tool might be super helpful. But she could also see the downsides. She's used heart rate variability measures, which are different, and really got sucked into the measuring without seeing much change. The focus became more about the measurement. I can see that being an issue.
Another said she'd rather rely on the felt sensations her body is communicating to her.

And another said yes and no. The measurement could lead to feeling defeated if she's not seeing change. Or maybe she'd feel inspired and treat it like an experiment, doing deliberate things and seeing what happens to her vagal efficiency.

blocks.p: There's no right or wrong answer here. Just reflect on it for yourself: would you like an objective measurement?
Then I took it a step further. If there was a magic pill that would activate your safety state, would you take it?

This would be different from a psychiatric medication. Psychiatric medications try to control behaviors or symptoms, but not the state in and of itself. So just playing pretend: if a pill would turn on your safety state, would you take it? Maybe your answer changes if you had to take it every day. Maybe it changes if it was a cure-all and you only had to take it once.
Or would you accept that no, this trauma recovery stuff is a long process, and you don't want the shortcut? You don't want to just activate it day after day by taking a magic pill.
If not, then you're kind of accepting that it's a long process. It takes practice. There is no hack that's going to get you there and keep you there day in, day out.
I think the best course is to first practice being in your safety state, and then, as your vagal brake strengthens enough, work on getting unstuck by directly feeling into your stuck defensive state.

You might be someone who'd reject the pill and also say no to any measures: "I can feel this stuff. I can feel myself in my safety state. I can notice when I have access to it, practice that day in, day out, dedicate myself to that practice, and really embrace the journey aspect of this." I think if you take the pill, you kind of lose the journey in a way.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: At the same time, I've heard from people who have used substances to get relief that it gave them a reference point for safety: a beautiful, wonderful experience they could call on or strive toward again. Maybe the ventral vagal magic pill would do that for you. Maybe it would give you a reference point for finally feeling safety.

Dr. Porges made a similar point on the podcast: "In the beginning, for many people, they don't know what safety feels like." ([Episode 254](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/20b541da-11ef-4b2e-b911-42b6ceba2bd1))

And that might be where you're at. You might be desperate enough to say, "I'll take the damn magic pill, because I need to feel something different from what I'm feeling now." I don't think there's anything wrong with that. It's not real anyway, but I don't think there's anything wrong with being desperate, or with wanting that reference point. Once you know what safety feels like, you have something you can keep subjectively measuring. You can keep striving for it, or at least you'll know when you don't have it. You'll know what truly feeling safe is like.

At the same time, it might dissuade you from your journey. If you go after that pill, or seek out that objective measure of ventral vagal activation or vagal efficiency, I wonder if it would deter you. I don't know. There's no one right answer.

I think the potential for measurement in the future is pretty cool. I'm interested in it. I like measurement. I like data stuff. But for me, and for the people I work with, what it ultimately comes down to is this:

ul: Can you feel safety or not?
Can you feel connected to the present moment?
Can you access your senses and experience them?
Can you look inward and experience what's inside of you without fear?

blocks.p: If the answer is yes to all of those, or some of them, or even one, that's a pretty good indication that you're on the right path, even without an objective measure and without a ventral vagal magic pill.

blocks.h: What your answer might tell you

blocks.p: This is all speculation, fun to think about, and maybe to journal about if you'd like. But I think your answers might indicate where you're at and what you need.

Maybe you do need something more objective. If your answer is, "Yes, I want to know my vagal efficiency," I can't give that to you, and you probably can't give it to yourself. But if you need more objectivity in your self-development or trauma recovery journey, maybe you can set that up for yourself. Maybe you track how often you feel something like calmness, or connected to the present moment. Maybe you create a spreadsheet and give yourself that objectivity. Maybe a clear goal makes it easier for you.

In my courses, I recommend that participants create a very clear, achievable, actionable, practical, measurable goal for themselves, something that's attainable and actually doable. I think it's important to have something to strive for. I don't think you need to be super objective about it and track it in a spreadsheet, but that might work for you. So if objectivity intrigues you, maybe it's time to set yourself up with something like that.

If the idea of a magic pill intrigues you, I don't blame you. It might indicate you're really desperate and ready for change, and there's nothing wrong with that at all. I would encourage you, though, to embrace the journey aspect of this if you haven't already. As much as you can, embrace that this is a long-term thing. It is a struggle. There is no hack. There is no shortcut, at least not that I know of.
So:

ol: Validate it. Yes, it's frustrating. Maybe you do feel desperate. Maybe you feel like giving up. Maybe you're pissed off. Validate your feelings.
Normalize it. Does it make sense that you feel the way you feel, based on the context of your life?
Give it permission. Give yourself permission to have those feelings.

blocks.p: And at the same time, maybe also accept that this is a process. It is a journey. There are obstacles, and there are successes as well.

As of right now, there is no objective measure, and I don't think there will ever be a magic pill for this, or any kind of pill. But who the heck knows? For now, these things don't exist, which means it really comes down to you. You can be more objective about it, but it really comes down to feeling your safety.
And if you can feel safety once, that means you can do it again. Then maybe you can build that into a practice, even just micro moments of mindfulness every day. I really recommend that.

Maybe you do want a quick fix, and you're not ready to embrace the journey aspect of this. That's okay. You're where you're at. Sadly, there is no magic pill for you. But you can set yourself up with some more objectivity in your journey.
